MONTREAL YMCA 


MISSION OF THE MONTREAL YMCA 


“The Montreal YMCA is a partnership of volunteers and 
staff committed to the fulfillment of people in spirit, 
mind and body and to the development of 
self-reliance in the individual and the community. 


Through its actions, programs and services, the 
Montreal YMCA reflects the needs and aspirations of 
communities and works with individuals, local 
communities and communities in developing countries 
in achieving social justice and control of their 
environments.”

MONTREAL YMCA 


1999-2000 


MESSAGE FROM THE CHAIRMAN OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS 
AND PRESIDENT & CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER 


The Montreal YMCA will celebrate its 150th anniversary next year. In preparation for the celebrations that 
will mark the event, we have spent some time this year reviewing our past. We were surprised to find that 
nostalgia was not the only part of the picture, but rather great pride in what the YMCA has become and the 
important role it plays in the lives of the people and communities it serves. 


Our quick look at the past confirmed that our "old" Association has stayed young. Maybe we didn't talk 
about building strong kids, strong families and strong communities 150 years ago, but we were already doing 
it then, just as we are today. 


In keeping with our charitable mission, the YMCA has committed much effort over the past few years towards 
offering its support to youth and families. The YMCA has helped people live more harmonious and healthy 
lives, and provided assistance to others who find little comfort in their own environment. 


It is clear that our response to the needs of the communities we serve are on target, since membership has 
never been so high and our community programs are increasingly in demand. This comes through loud and 
clear in the overview of activities in our centres. 


In closing, we wish to thank the volunteers and staff in our eleven centres, as well as the members of our 
Board of Directors and the Montreal YMCA Foundation for their commitment, energy and open minds. In 
fact, they have made this an exceptional year, because the Downtown YMCA will have its new building, and 
we have the strength to build for our future. 


Whad haf 


Paul Dunne Michael Weil 
Chairman of the Board President and Chief Executive Officer 


At the Heart of Community Life 


DOWNTOWN YMCA - First Stop 


On September 2, 1999, an information and referral centre called First Stop was set up in the 
downtown bus terminal. Twelve hours a day, 365 days a year, two professionals circulate 
throughout the bus station, and strike up conversations with recent arrivals to Montreal who appear 
vulnerable. 


First Stop helps approximately 150 travellers every month: young runaways, seniors who seem 
confused, people with mental health problems, immigrants, refugees, as well as tourists who have 
lost their baggage. People needing help are directed to various community services, hospitals or 
other centres where they can find shelter, a meal, clothing, care or assistance. 


Created through a partnership of the Downtown YMCA, Passages and Le Bon Dieu dans la Rue, First 
Stop benefits from the cooperation of numerous organizations: bus terminal management, Station 
21 police, Centraide, the National Crime Prevention Centre, the Ministére de la Sécurité publique du 
Québec, the Ministére de la Santé et des Services sociaux (youth protection services), the Regional 
Health and Social Services Board of Montreal and the City of Montreal. 


YMCA DU PARC - A Pillar of Community Development 


The Du Parc YMCA has made community development a top priority. In addition to creating its own 
programs, the centre has spent the past few years forming partnerships with social groups, public 
organizations and local merchants. Its goal is to find solutions to problems, such as exclusion, 
poverty and isolation. Its approach is to foster local, sustainable development through 
self-empowerment and partnerships. 


In the 1999-2000 year alone, the Du Parc YMCA supported fifteen community projects outside its 
walls. For example, the centre is represented on the Board of Directors of Action Solidarité 
Grand-Plateau, the St-Louis and Mile-End multi-sectoral committee, youth and early childhood 
committees set up by the CLSC, and Loges du Mile-End (a public housing project) as well as the 
Mile-End artists’ co-op. In addition, the Du Parc YMCA sponsors the local Tandem and Eco-Quartier 
programs, which are also very active in the community, especially with the community garden and 
senior citizens’ committee to promote the safety of women. 


GUY-FAVREAU YMCA - A Helping Hand 


In the Centre-South Montreal, one of the most underprivileged areas of the city, the Guy-Favreau 
YMCA works hard to help the local population improve living conditions. 


Since education is the key to the future, the centre formed a partnership with a local school to 
collect school supplies for elementary students from low-income families. 


Every two weeks, the Guy-Favreau YMCA holds a free legal clinic. This year, 156 people took 
advantage of a free 20-minute consultation to find out more about their legal rights in the areas of 
family, business, immigration, housing, and contract law, as well as other types of law. 


The Guy-Favreau YMCA offers free prenatal swimming classes to pregnant teenage girls in the 
community. The centre also provides free space to numerous local community groups where they 
can hold their activities. A large part of the programs are financed through the tireless efforts of 
our community programs coordinator, Pierre Méthot. 


At the Heart of Community Life 


HOCHELAGA-MAISONNEUVE YMCA - 
Young Community Leader Award 


As proof of its conviction that every youth has ideals, the Hochelaga-Maisonneuve YMCA annually 
celebrates the exceptional commitment and leadership of a youth between the ages of 13 and 17. 


This year’s Young Community Leader Award was presented to Mélina Dubois, a highly dynamic young 
woman who is full of ideas on how to prevent violence. She also gives a voice to teens around her. 
Mélina hosts a radio show on CIBL called “Des jeunes qui ont de la gueule”, where she gives youth 
a chance to express themselves on air and interviews community program coordinators about their 
youth programs. Mélina is also a member of the “Manifeste ta paix” youth group, which meets every 
week to find solutions to violence. Their recommendations will be published in the form of a 
manifesto. 


Bravo Mélina! Keep up the good work! 


NDG YMCA - Graffiti Brigade 

The City of Montreal selected the NDG YMCA to set up a social reintegration program financed by 
the Federal government. The purpose of the program is to help youth who are experiencing social or 
financial difficulties to acquire the necessary skills to hold down a job. In the program’s first year, 
the YMCA provided training to ten unemployed and out-of-school youths from the community. One 
year later, three more YMCA centres were selected to become involved in the program, namely; 
Pointe Ste-Charles, Du Parc and Downtown. 


The youths approached local merchants to offer graffiti removal services. Through workshops and 
practical training, they learned how to draw up a contract and organize their work. Graffiti Brigade 
members were also made aware of general work requirements, such as punctuality, behaviour, and so 
on. The program achieved a 90% success rate, since most of the youths found a job or went back 
to school. A good number of them maintained their ties with the YMCA by joining the Youth Centre 
or volunteering for special events. 


POINTE SAINT-CHARLES YMCA - Friday Night Hockey League 


The Friday night hockey league, better known as the Mid-Nite Hockey League, was created to 
counter increased drug and alcohol abuse among youth in Pointe-Saint-Charles. Every Friday, 
between 8 p.m. and midnight, the YMCA offers youth an alternative to the streets. For the past 
four years, youth have been given the opportunity to develop qualities such as team spirit and 
commitment in a leisure environment. 


The league brings together some 60 teens and young adults for a season that runs from October to 
May and includes regular games, play-offs, an all-star game and hockey meets with surrounding 
communities. The season culminates in an awards night where trophies and medals are presented 
to various league members. 


The league is partially financed through an annual benefit event. 


SAINT-LAURENT YMCA - Toy Library 


Only one year after its creation, the toy library has doubled its membership objective with 50 
member families. The service, which works the same way as a library, gives lower-income families 
access to stimulating games and toys in a creative and safe environment. 


Aside from lending games and toys, the toy library aims to provide an environment that fosters 
family growth and dialogue. It offers information workshops for parents on children’s changing 
needs and focuses on the importance of play in their development. The toy library also teaches 
children to respect what they borrow. 


Over the next few years, the toy library plans to encourage parental participation in its organization 
and management, as well as in training volunteers and recruiting more families in the 
underprivileged Norgate-Crevier area. The toy library will also work to strengthen its partnerships 
and secure adequate funding. 


the Heart of Community Life 


WEST ISLAND YMCA - Youth Centre 


The West Island Youth Centre is finally here! Citizens have been waiting for a youth centre in this 
part of town for years, which once again proves how effective partnerships can be. 


The Youth Centre is the result of the West Island YMCA Community Programs Centre’s involvement in 
a street work program. The centre was able to start up with financial support from Centraide and 
the cooperation of the following organizations: 

- West Island Volunteer Bureau 

-  CLSC Lac St-Louis 

- YMCA 

- City of Pointe-Claire 

-  MUC Police Service - Station 5 

- Carrefour jeunesse emploi 


Youth are slowly beginning to add their personal touch to the centre by decorating the walls with 
their paintings, and working with programming staff to develop programs that will meet their 
specific needs. 


WESTMOUNT YMCA - The Road to Integration 


Until 1997, the Westmount YMCA had only a very limited number of children with special needs in 
its preschool and youth programs. 


Staff and volunteers then decided to take things in hand and firmly resolved to foster integration. 
Since then, an integration specialist has been hired every summer to train volunteers and staff, 
while ensuring that the needs of all children are met. 


This summer's day camp welcomed 69 children with special needs. As is the case every year, the 
experience proved beneficial for all - both big and small - with or without a disability. Mainstream 
children learned to accept differences and recognize the value of all children around them. Once 
surrounded by other children and volunteers, children with a disability blossomed and learned how 
to participate fully in activities. Volunteers and camp counsellors had the pleasure of helping bring 
a smile to the faces of these very special children. 


The integration program is supported by the Douglas Hospital, Batshaw Youth Services and the 
Giant Steps group. 


KAMP KANAWANA - A Camp for People of All Ages 


This year, Kamp Kanawana welcomed campers between the ages of 3 and 60 from numerous 
organizations. A total of 1150 people participated in our summer rental and camp programs alone. 
We also opened our doors to groups from organizations other than the YMCA, including the Allan 
Memorial Institute and various Montreal school boards. 


On a more practical note, we acquired new equipment for our canoe tripping, archery and sailing 
programs. Through a donation of wood supplies from Goodfellow Wood and Lumber, we improved 
our facilities by building new picnic tables and two new cabins, as well as rebuilding decks and 
stairs. 


Any unused items were distributed at the end of the season. Unclaimed articles in the lost and 
found were sent to Le Bon Dieu dans la Rue and the Downtown YMCA refugee program. Food was 
sent to soup kitchens and shelters. 


Next year, we plan to offer winter camps during the holiday season and spring break. 


INTERNATIONAL PROGRAMS - Compafieros Sin Fronteras 


In the 1999 - 2000 year, there were several exchanges between the YMCAs of Montreal, El Salvador, 
Honduras, Nicaragua and Ecuador that proved enriching for all. A number of youth and young 
adults volunteered for periods of one to six months as part of the Mano a Mano sin Fronteras 
program and Canadian International Development Agency (CIDA) initiatives. 


In addition, the organization Development and Peace financed a $75,000 agricultural diversification 
project submitted by the Montreal YMCA on behalf of the Honduras YMCA to help the country 
recover from Hurricane Mitch. 


This year’s activities saw a growing interest in international cooperation on the part of our staff 
and volunteers. The Montreal YMCA is, indeed, thinking globally and acting locally!

1999-2000 MONTREAL YMCA SOCIAL RESULTS 


Through its programs and activities, the Montreal YMCA reached 107,082 
people in 1999-2000. 


In 1999-2000, the Montreal YMCA facilitated access to its programs and 
services for more than 4,500 people who were in financial difficulty.

MONTREAL YMCA FOUNDATION 


1999-2000 


MESSAGE FROM THE CHAIRMAN OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS 
AND PRESIDENT OF THE MONTREAL YMCA FOUNDATION 


The role of the Foundation is to ensure long-term funding for the Montreal YMCA so all of our centres can play a 


front-line role in the community, while providing access to all of our programs. 


Through its Campaign Committee, the Foundation pursued its efforts this year to revitalize the YMCA’s downtown 
facilities. Construction began on schedule at the end of the fall and is progressing smoothly. Everything should 


be completed in time for the YMCA’s 150th anniversary celebrations in 2001. 


The Campaign was a success in financial terms, since we have nearly reached our objective of $20 million. More 
importantly, it gave us the opportunity to strengthen our ties with neighbours and members. The dialogue 


spawned by the Campaign is sure to generate long-term benefits for the entire Association. 


Another less spectacular but equally important change in keeping with the times is the reorganization of our 
Board of Directors. The Board went from 40 to 24 seats this year, and a series of task-specific volunteer 


committees were created in the process. 


Once again this year, the Foundation worked extremely hard and has numerous accomplishments to its credit. 
We wish to thank our Board Members, as well as the Revitalization Campaign Committee members and all the 
volunteers who helped with the Campaign. In addition, we wish to thank the staff of the Montreal YMCA 


Foundation who provided input to the Board and implemented its decisions. 


CLibconte 


Claude A. Garcia Marcel Coté 


Chairman of the Board President

The amount was used to finance several Montreal YMCA youth programs.
